blocks.text: The System Design Interview Framework
The 45-minute playbook for any system design interview: scope first, sketch together, deep-dive where it hurts, and land the wrap-up — with the anti-patterns that sink candidates.
Why this matters

Here's the secret nobody tells you before your first system design interview: there is no right answer. The interviewer isn't holding a reference diagram behind the whiteboard, waiting to see if yours matches. They're watching something else entirely — how you handle a problem nobody fully specified, with a stranger, under time pressure, out loud.

That's the whole game. A system design interview is a simulation of the job: a senior engineer walks into your office with a vague problem — "notifications are falling over, we need to rethink it" — and you figure it out together. The interview compresses that into 45 minutes and grades the collaboration, not the boxes.
Once you see it that way, the fear drains out of it. You're not taking an exam. You're planning a road trip with a friend — and this lesson is the map.
Picture a road trip

This lesson's running analogy: you and a friend are planning a road trip, and you have to leave in 45 minutes. You'd never just grab the keys and start driving. First you'd agree on the destination, who's coming, and the budget — that's scoping. Then you'd sketch the route on a map together and make sure your friend nods along — that's the high-level design with buy-in. Then you'd zoom in on the hard legs: the mountain pass, the stretch with no gas stations — that's the deep dive. And before you pull out of the driveway, you'd read the plan back: "so we're taking I-70, fueling in Denver, cabin by six" — that's the wrap-up.
The destination is the requirements: what are we actually building?
The sketched route is the high-level design: the boxes and arrows everyone agrees on.
The mountain pass is the deep dive: the one component where the interview is won or lost.
Reading the plan back is the wrap-up: the summary that proves you were driving, not just riding along.
And the 45-minute departure time is real. Spend the whole morning debating snacks and you never leave the driveway. Every anti-pattern in this lesson is a version of missing the departure.
What the interviewer is actually grading
Interviewers score four things, roughly in this order:

Communication. Did you think out loud? Could a stranger follow your reasoning? Silence is the only true failure mode — a quiet genius and an empty chair look identical from the interviewer's side of the table.

Scoping. Did you pin down the problem before solving it? The candidate who asks "are we talking hundreds of notifications a day, or hundreds of millions?" before drawing a single box is already ahead. Engineers who clarify first are engineers who don't build the wrong thing for six months.

Trade-off reasoning. Every real decision has a cost. "We chose X because Y, accepting Z" is the sentence that gets offers. Candidates who present one option as obviously correct sound like they've never operated anything at 2 a.m.

Technical depth, applied sparingly. You need to go deep somewhere — one component, done properly. The key generator, not the login page. Depth everywhere is impossible in 45 minutes, and trying looks like panic.

Notice what's missing: the "correct" architecture. Two strong candidates can draw different diagrams and both pass, because both showed judgment. The diagram is the artifact; the thinking is the product.
Step 1 — Agree on the destination (3–10 minutes)
Goal: leave this step with a written scope both of you accept: what the system does, at what scale, and what you're explicitly not building.

How to execute it. Ask questions before you draw anything. The best candidates treat the opening minutes like checking the destination, the passenger list, and the fuel budget before touching the keys: functional requirements first ("what are the core features?"), then scale ("how many users? reads vs writes?"), then constraints ("web, mobile, or both? any latency targets?"). Write the answers down where the interviewer can see them — the whiteboard is shared memory, and pointing back at it later ("remember we agreed reads outnumber writes 100 to 1? that's why I'm caching here") is enormously persuasive. Then state your assumptions out loud and get a nod: "I'm assuming 10 million daily users and a 100-to-1 read ratio — sound fair?" An assumption the interviewer blessed is a decision you don't have to defend later.
Time-box: 3–10 minutes. Closer to 3 for a familiar problem, up to 10 if the prompt is genuinely ambiguous. If you're still clarifying at minute 15, you're not being thorough — you're stalling.
Anti-patterns:
Grabbing the keys. Drawing boxes before the scope is agreed. The most common failure in system design interviews, and it's fatal: everything downstream inherits the wrong destination.
The interrogation. Twenty rapid-fire questions with no synthesis. Ask in clusters, then summarize: "so — short links and redirects, 100M new URLs a month, analytics out of scope. Correct?"

Scope creep by politeness. "Should I also handle custom aliases? Expiring links? QR codes?" Every yes doubles your remaining work. Park extras explicitly: "I'll note analytics as a follow-up and keep it out of the core design."
Step 2 — Sketch the route together (10–15 minutes)
Goal: a high-level diagram — clients, API, core services, data stores, cache — that the interviewer has visibly bought into.

How to execute it. Draw the simple version first. Monolith-ish is fine as a starting sketch; what matters is that you narrate as you draw ("requests come in here, the API fans out to these two services, reads hit the cache first"). Then do the back-of-envelope math against the scope from Step 1 — two minutes of arithmetic that tells you which boxes actually need to be distributed and which are fine as single instances. Walk one request end to end through the sketch ("a user shortens a URL: POST hits the API, the key service mints a ticket, we write the mapping, return the short link") and watch for the moment something in your sketch can't answer the walkthrough — that's your deep-dive target revealing itself. And get the buy-in explicitly: "does this high-level picture look right before I go deeper on the key generator?" An interviewer who said yes is now collaborating, not judging.
Time-box: 10–15 minutes, including the estimation math. This is the step candidates rush — they want to get to the "impressive" deep dive. Resist it. A shaky sketch makes the deep dive irrelevant.
Anti-patterns:
The silent cartographer. Drawing for six minutes without a word. Narrate continuously — the interviewer can't grade thinking they can't hear.

Alphabet-soup architecture. Kafka, Redis, Cassandra on the board in minute two, before any requirement justifies them. Brand names are not design. If you can't say why a component earns its place, it doesn't.
Skipping the math. A high-level design with no numbers is a drawing, not engineering. The two-minute estimate is what separates "boxes" from "a system."
Designing alone. Never asking "does this look right?" turns a collaboration back into an exam — and you're grading yourself.
Step 3 — Drive the hard legs (10–25 minutes)
Goal: go deep on one or two components where the problem actually lives, showing trade-off judgment under pressure.

How to execute it. You can't go deep everywhere — that's the point. Pick the component the walkthrough exposed: the key generator in a URL shortener, the fan-out path in a news feed, the ordering guarantee in chat. Name the options honestly (there are always two or three credible ones), compare them on the criteria the scope demands, and pick one for stated reasons: "I'm choosing the dedicated key service over hashing because our write path can't afford a collision check on every insert at this scale, and I'm accepting the extra service to operate." Then chase the failure modes the interviewer will probe: what happens when this component dies, what happens at 10× the traffic, where's the bottleneck. Let the interviewer steer — if they keep asking about the cache, the cache is the interview now. Follow them.
Time-box: 10–25 minutes. This is the biggest block because it's the substance. But it's capped: at minute 35 you must be wrapping up, no matter how interesting the mountain pass is.
Anti-patterns:
Rabbit-holing. Fifteen minutes on the perfect cache-eviction policy while the database design is a blank box. Depth is scored per component chosen wisely, not per minute spent.
The tourist. Touching every component for ninety seconds each. That's Step 2 repeated louder, not a deep dive.

Defending instead of reasoning. Folding at the first pushback — or the opposite, clinging to a choice the interviewer just falsified. The graded move is: acknowledge the objection, adjust the design, state the new trade-off. Flexibility under pressure is the job.

Over-engineering the pass. Designing for a billion users when the scope said ten million. Match the depth to the scope you agreed in Step 1 — the interviewer is watching whether you remember your own destination.
Step 3 is graded on trade-off reasoning — the "we chose X because Y, accepting Z" sentence. If you want to hear what world-class trade-off reasoning sounds like, spend an hour with Martin Kleppmann:
Step 4 — Read the route back (3–5 minutes)
Goal: a crisp summary that proves the design hangs together, plus honest notes on what you'd do with more time.

How to execute it. With a few minutes left, stop designing and summarize: the scope, the key decisions and why, the component you went deep on, the trade-offs you accepted. Then name the follow-ups yourself before the interviewer does — "with more time I'd add analytics as a separate pipeline, harden the key service's failover, and load-test the redirect path." Ending on self-identified improvements signals something powerful: you know the design isn't perfect, and you know exactly where it isn't. That's senior-engineer behavior.
Time-box: 3–5 minutes. Start watching the clock at minute 35 and reserve the ending deliberately. The summary is not leftover time — it's a scheduled stop.
Anti-patterns:
Trailing off. "...and yeah, that's basically it?" A design with no summary reads as a design the candidate couldn't hold in their head.

The surprise feature. Introducing a brand-new component in the wrap-up ("oh, and we'd add a message queue here"). If it wasn't in the design, it doesn't exist. Mention it as a follow-up or not at all.
Apologizing for the design. "This probably wouldn't work at real scale but…" — you scoped it, you reasoned it, stand behind it. Name limitations as engineering facts, not confessions.
The 45-minute map
Here's the whole trip on one dashboard. Print it mentally; glance at the clock at each boundary.
Step, What you're doing, Minutes, You're done when
1. Agree on the destination, Clarify requirements, fix scope, state assumptions, 3–10, Both of you accept a written scope
2. Sketch the route, High-level diagram, back-of-envelope math, walkthrough, buy-in, 10–15, Interviewer nods at the sketch
3. Drive the hard legs, Deep dive on 1–2 components, trade-offs, failure modes, 10–25, One component designed properly, objections handled
4. Read the route back, Summary, decisions recap, follow-ups, 3–5, You stop with time to spare, not because time ran out

Two things to notice. First, the steps feed each other: the scope justifies the sketch, the sketch's walkthrough picks the deep-dive target, the summary replays all three. A candidate who treats them as separate phases — clarifying, then forgetting the scope — loses the thread. Second, the clock is a design constraint like any other. Managing it visibly ("we're at 20 minutes, let me lock the sketch and go deep on the key generator") is itself a scored skill: it's what running a real design review feels like.
Your question bank
You don't need brilliant improvised questions. You need a bank of reliable ones, sorted by problem family. Steal these; they're yours now.
Every problem, always:
What are the two or three core features? Everything else is a follow-up.
What's the scale — users, reads per second, writes per second?
What's the read-to-write ratio? (This one number shapes more designs than any other.)
Web, mobile, or both? Any latency targets?
Storage-heavy (Drive, photo sharing, URL shortener):
How much data per user, and how long do we keep it?
How much of it is hot vs archival? (The answer decides your storage tiers.)
Do we need strong durability guarantees, or is best-effort acceptable?
Read-heavy (news feed, search, CDN-shaped problems):
How fresh must reads be — seconds, minutes, "eventually"?
What's the fan-out shape: a few celebrities with millions of followers, or everyone roughly equal? (The whale problem lives here.)
Cacheable? What's the hit ratio likely to be?
Real-time / interactive (chat, collaborative editing, live location):
What latency is "real-time" here — under 100 ms, under a second?
How many concurrent connections, not just total users?
What happens on disconnect — resume, replay, or start over?
Analytics / aggregation (ad clicks, metrics pipelines):
Is this streaming or batch — do we need answers in seconds, or is tomorrow fine?
Event time or processing time? (Late-arriving data is the whole problem.)
Approximate answers acceptable, or must every count be exact?
Ask in clusters of two or three, then summarize back. The bank gets you started; the summary proves you listened.
Watch it run: TinyURL in 45 minutes
Let's drive the whole route on a problem you know — Design a URL Shortener. Listen for what each step sounds like.

Minutes 0–7 — the destination. "So the core is two operations: shorten a long URL, redirect a short one back. Let me fix the scale: say 100 million new URLs a month? And reads outnumber writes — ten redirects per URL? I'll assume web and mobile both, no strict latency target beyond snappy redirects. Analytics, custom aliases, expiring links — I'll park those as follow-ups, not day-one scope. Fair?" The interviewer nods. Destination agreed, in six minutes.

Minutes 7–20 — the sketch. You draw client, API, key service, database, cache. Then the math, out loud: "100 million a month is about 40 writes a second — writes are trivial. Reads are 400 a second average, maybe a thousand at peak. Ten-to-one read-heavy, so the redirect path gets the cache budget. Storage: 12 billion URLs over ten years at about 500 bytes each is about 6 TB — shardable, no heroics needed." You walk one shorten and one redirect through the boxes. "Does this high-level picture look right before I go deeper?" Nod. Route sketched, math done, buy-in secured.

Minutes 20–38 — the hard leg. The walkthrough exposed it: key generation is the crux. "Three options: hash the URL, a shared counter, or a dedicated key service. Hashing gives free dedup but every insert pays a collision check. The counter is simple but it's a single choke point — and sequential keys are enumerable, anyone could scrape every link. I'll take the dedicated key service: each server mints from its own slice of the keyspace and app servers fetch keys in batches. I'm accepting one more service to operate in exchange for no coordination on the write path." The interviewer pushes: "what if a key server dies?" You adjust: slices are pre-allocated, a dead server's slice just sits unused until recovery — no other server can mint its keys, so no duplicates, only reduced capacity. Trade-off stated, objection absorbed.

Minutes 38–43 — read it back. "So: shorten and redirect at 100M URLs a month, read-heavy ten to one. API fronting a key service with disjoint keyspace slices, sharded mapping store, cache on the redirect path. Deep dive was key generation — batch-minted keys, no per-write coordination, dead servers fail safe. With more time: analytics as a separate pipeline, and I'd load-test the redirect path at 10× before trusting the cache sizing." Done with two minutes to spare. That's what passing sounds like.

Notice the back-of-envelope moment in Step 2 — forty writes a second, 6 TB over ten years. That two-minute calculation is what told the candidate the redirect path deserved the cache and the database didn't need heroics. Estimation isn't a party trick; it's how the sketch earns the word "design." (The full technique gets its own lesson — the upcoming back-of-envelope reference.) Dos and don'ts
Do:
Think out loud, always. Narrate the reasoning, not just the conclusions. "I'm choosing X because…" is the highest-value sentence in the interview.
Treat the interviewer as your road-trip friend. Ask, check, adjust. Collaboration is scored; solo brilliance is invisible.
Write the scope down and point at it. The whiteboard is shared memory — use it to anchor later decisions.
Name trade-offs explicitly. Every "we chose X" needs its "accepting Y." That's the sound of experience.
Manage the clock visibly. Calling out the time shows you can run a meeting, not just a whiteboard.
End early rather than trail off. A crisp finish beats a design that dies at minute 45 mid-sentence.
Don't:
Don't go silent. Six quiet minutes of drawing is six minutes of zero signal. If you're thinking, say you're thinking.
Don't start driving before the destination is agreed. Boxes before scope is the classic fail.
Don't name-drop infrastructure. Kafka doesn't earn points; justified Kafka does.
Don't defend a falsified choice. When the interviewer breaks your design, thank the breakage — adjusting under pressure is the job.
Don't gold-plate. Designing for a billion users when the scope said ten million is not ambition, it's not listening.
Don't apologize for the design. Limitations are engineering facts. State them, don't confess them.
Takeaways
A system design interview grades collaboration under ambiguity — communication, scoping, and trade-off reasoning — not the "right" diagram.

Run the four steps in order: agree on the destination (scope, 3–10 min), sketch the route and get buy-in (high-level + math, 10–15 min), drive the hard legs (deep dive on 1–2 components, 10–25 min), read the route back (summary + follow-ups, 3–5 min).

Each step has a signature failure: grabbing the keys (drawing before scoping), the silent cartographer (drawing without narrating), rabbit-holing (depth in the wrong place), trailing off (no summary). Learn their shapes so you can catch yourself mid-step.
Keep a clarifying-question bank by problem family and ask in clusters — then summarize back to prove you listened.
The back-of-envelope math in Step 2 is what turns boxes into a design: two minutes of arithmetic decides where the engineering budget goes.
Manage the clock out loud. Starting the wrap-up at minute 38 on purpose is a scored skill.
